subject: Maths
title: Year 9 Maths Exam 7
intro: You may use a calculator. Show your working in the working box: method marks are given even when the final answer is wrong. Round only at the end, and give answers to the accuracy the question asks for.

questions.q: Which value of x satisfies both x > 2.5 and x ≤ 4?
questions.ms: B1: 4. 2.5 is not included (> not ≥), 4 is included (≤), 4.5 is too big.
B1: x = 7 or x = −1.5. Set each bracket to 0: 2x + 3 = 0 gives x = −3 ÷ 2 = −1.5.

questions.q: Which describes the graph of y = −2x2 + 5x + 3?
questions.ms: B1: ∩-shaped with a maximum point, because the x² term is negative. It crosses the y-axis at +3.

questions.q:
A lift can carry at most 400 kg. Four people are already inside. They weigh 72.5 kg, 85.3 kg, 68.4 kg and 91.8 kg.
Write an inequality and solve it to find the maximum weight of a fifth person who gets in. (kg)
questions.ms: Answer: 82 kg. M1 for 318 + w ≤ 400 (adding the four weights to get 318). M1 for w ≤ 82. A1 for 82 kg.

questions.q:
n is an integer.
5n + 3 ≥ 2n − 9 and 4n − 7 < 2(n + 1)
List all the values of n that satisfy both inequalities.
questions.hint: Type the values from smallest to largest, separated by commas, like -2,0,3
questions.ms: Answer: −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. M1 for 3n ≥ −12 so n ≥ −4. M1 for 2n < 9 so n < 4.5. A1 for the full list (−4 is included; 5 is too big).

questions.q:
A taxi charges a fixed fee of £3.50 plus £1.80 for every kilometre. Leila has £25 and travels d km.
Write down an inequality in terms of d to show that Leila can afford the journey.
questions.ms: Answer: 3.5 + 1.8d ≤ 25. B1 (≤ because she can spend exactly £25).

questions.q: Find the greatest whole number of kilometres Leila can travel. (km)
questions.ms: Answer: 11 km. M1 for 1.8d ≤ 21.5 so d ≤ 11.94… A1 for 11 (round down: 12 km would cost £25.10, which is too much).

questions.q: Expand and simplify (2x + 1)(x − 3)(x + 2).
questions.ms: Answer: 2x³ − x² − 13x − 6. M1 for expanding two brackets, e.g. (2x + 1)(x − 3) = 2x² − 5x − 3. M1 for multiplying by the third bracket with at least 4 correct terms out of 6 (2x³ + 4x² − 5x² − 10x − 3x − 6). A1 cao.

questions.q: Factorise 6x2 − 7x − 20.
questions.ms: Answer: (3x + 4)(2x − 5). M1 for 6x² − 15x + 8x − 20, or brackets that give two of the three terms. A1. Check: a × c = −120, and −15 × 8 = −120, −15 + 8 = −7.

questions.q: Factorise fully 12x2 − 27.
questions.ms: Answer: 3(2x − 3)(2x + 3). M1 for 3(4x² − 9). A1 for the difference of two squares: 4x² − 9 = (2x)² − 3². Common mistake: stopping at 3(4x² − 9).

questions.q:
Solve 2x2 − 5x − 9 = 0. Give your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
x = −b ± √(b2 − 4ac)2a
questions.hint: Type both answers separated by a comma, like 3,-2
questions.ms: Answer: x = 3.71 or x = −1.21. M1 for correct substitution (a = 2, b = −5, c = −9), so x = (5 ± √(25 + 72)) ÷ 4. M1 for √97 or 9.84… A1 for both answers.

questions.q:
Omar uses the quadratic formula to solve an equation of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0. He correctly writes
x = −7 ± √(49 − 24)6
Find the values of a, b and c, and write down Omar's equation.

A ball is kicked upwards. Its height, h metres, after t seconds is h = 20t − 4.9t2.
Find the maximum height of the ball. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (m)
questions.ms: Answer: 20.4 m. M1 for the ball landing at t = 20 ÷ 4.9 = 4.08… M1 for the top at t = 2.04… (halfway). A1 for 20.4.

questions.q: For how long is the ball at least 15 m above the ground? Give your answer to 2 decimal places. (seconds)
questions.ms: Answer: 2.10 seconds. M1 for 4.9t² − 20t + 15 = 0. M1 for correct substitution into the quadratic formula (√106 = 10.29…). A1 for t = 0.99… and t = 3.09… A1 for 2.10 (accept 2.1).

questions.q:
A rectangular pool is 25 m long and 10 m wide. A path x m wide goes all the way round the pool. The total area of the pool and path is 400 m2.
Show that 2x2 + 35x − 75 = 0.
questions.ms: M1 for the new length (25 + 2x) and width (10 + 2x). M1 for (25 + 2x)(10 + 2x) = 400 expanded to 250 + 70x + 4x² = 400. A1 for 4x² + 70x − 150 = 0, then dividing by 2 to get 2x² + 35x − 75 = 0 (every step shown).

questions.q: Solve 2x2 + 35x − 75 = 0 to find the width of the path. Give your answer to 2 decimal places. (m)
questions.ms: Answer: 1.93 m. M1 for correct substitution into the formula: x = (−35 ± √(1225 + 600)) ÷ 4. A1 for x = 1.93 and x = −19.43. A1 for choosing 1.93 m and rejecting −19.43 because a width cannot be negative.

questions.q:
The curve y = 2x2 − 4x − 30 is drawn.
Find the x-coordinates where the curve crosses the x-axis.
questions.hint: Type both answers separated by a comma, like 3,-2
questions.ms: Answer: x = 5 and x = −3. M1 for 2(x² − 2x − 15) = 0 or 2(x − 5)(x + 3) = 0. A1 for both.

questions.q: Write down the y-coordinate where the curve crosses the y-axis.
questions.ms: Answer: −30. B1: put x = 0, so y = −30.

questions.q: Find the coordinates of the turning point of the curve.
questions.ms: Answer: (1, −32). M1 for x = 1 (halfway between −3 and 5). A1 for y = 2 − 4 − 30 = −32.

questions.q:
Solve 3(x + 2)2 = 5(x + 2).
Give all the solutions.
questions.hint: Type both answers separated by a comma, like 1/2,-3
questions.ms: Answer: x = −2 or x = −1/3. M1 for (x + 2)(3(x + 2) − 5) = 0, or expanding to 3x² + 7x + 2 = 0. M1 for (x + 2)(3x + 1) = 0. A1 for both (accept −0.33). Common mistake: dividing both sides by (x + 2), which loses x = −2.

questions.q: Solve 3x2 − 5x − 2 ≤ 0
questions.hint: Type it like x>4 or -2= for ≥)
questions.ms: Answer: −1/3 ≤ x ≤ 2. M1 for (3x + 1)(x − 2). A1 for critical values −1/3 and 2. M1 for choosing the region between the roots (a U-shaped curve is below the x-axis between its roots). A1 for −1/3 ≤ x ≤ 2.

questions.q: Prove that (3n + 1)2 − (3n − 1)2 is a multiple of 12 for every integer n.
questions.ms: M1 for expanding one bracket correctly: 9n² + 6n + 1 or 9n² − 6n + 1. M1 for 12n. A1 for a statement: 12n = 12 × n, so it is a multiple of 12. Numerical examples only: 0 marks.

questions.q: Prove that the difference between the squares of any two consecutive integers is always odd.
questions.ms: M1 for (n + 1)² − n². M1 for n² + 2n + 1 − n² = 2n + 1. A1 for a statement: 2n is even, so 2n + 1 is odd. Numerical examples only: 0 marks.

questions.q:
Amal says: “n2 − n + 11 is a prime number for every positive whole number n.”
Show that Amal is wrong.
questions.ms: B1 for choosing n = 11 (or another value that works, e.g. n = 12 gives 143 = 11 × 13). B1 for showing the result is not prime: 121 − 11 + 11 = 121 = 11 × 11. Testing only values that give primes: 0 marks.
